note: Public 20-question sample of draft RPSGT questions under review. Tracings are original.

questions.stem: A patient's Epworth Sleepiness Scale total is 17. This score is best described as
questions.rationale: ESS totals of 16 to 24 indicate severe excessive sleepiness. Scores of 10 or less are normal and 11 to 12 are mild. The ESS rates sleepiness only; it cannot diagnose any disorder.

questions.stem: During setup, a patient lists sertraline, an SSRI antidepressant, among daily medications. Which effect on tonight's recording should the technologist anticipate and note?
options: Fewer periodic limb movements than usual
Suppressed REM sleep and possible REM without atonia
More slow-wave sleep and fewer arousals
Sleep-onset REM periods on every nap
questions.rationale: SSRIs suppress REM sleep, lengthen REM latency, and can cause REM sleep without atonia and increased periodic limb movements. They do not increase slow-wave sleep or cause SOREMPs; abrupt withdrawal of REM-suppressing drugs, not their use, can cause REM rebound.
questions.reference: Wichniak A, et al. Effects of antidepressants on sleep. Curr Psychiatry Rep. 2017;19(9):63.

questions.stem: A patient scheduled for an MSLT asks what will happen during the day. The technologist should explain that the patient will
options: stay awake in a dark room for 8 hours.
sleep through the morning and leave at noon.
take 5 scheduled naps about 2 hours apart and stay awake between them.
nap whenever they feel tired during the day.
questions.rationale: The MSLT is five nap opportunities at 2-hour intervals, starting 1.5 to 3 hours after the overnight study ends. Between naps, the patient must stay out of bed and awake, avoid caffeine and bright sunlight, and not smoke for 30 minutes before each nap.
questions.reference: Littner MR, et al. Sleep. 2005;28(1):113-121.

questions.stem: An overweight patient with moderate OSA asks whether losing weight could help. Which response is most accurate?
options: Weight loss often lowers the AHI and is advised along with other treatment.
Body weight has little effect on how severe sleep apnea becomes.
Losing about 5 pounds is enough to cure most cases of sleep apnea.
Weight loss usually cures sleep apnea, so CPAP can stop right away.
questions.rationale: Weight loss commonly reduces OSA severity and is recommended for overweight or obese patients, but it rarely cures moderate OSA on its own and takes time, so other treatment continues. Any change in weight may change the pressure needed.
questions.reference: Hudgel DW, et al. The role of weight management in the treatment of adult OSA: an ATS clinical practice guideline. Am J Respir Crit Care Med. 2018;198(6):e70-e87.

questions.stem: The epoch shown is recorded during the first hour of a study. Which action should the technologist take FIRST?
options: Check the impedance of the O2 and M1 electrodes and re-prep as needed
Turn on the 60 Hz notch filter for all channels
Lower the high-frequency filter on O2-M1 to 15 Hz
Ignore it, because it only affects one channel
questions.rationale: A thick, uniform band on one channel is 60 Hz line interference, usually caused by a high-impedance or loose electrode. The fix is to correct the electrode. A notch filter is a last resort, and lowering the high-frequency filter distorts EEG.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3; standard PSG technology texts.

image.alt: N2 epoch with a thick, uniform, fuzzy band obscuring the O2-M1 channel; other channels look normal.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Thick, even band of fast activity on O2-M1 only. Every other channel is clean, which points to one bad electrode.

evidence.takeaway: Line noise on a single channel means a high-impedance or loose electrode. Fix O2 or M1 before reaching for the notch filter.

questions.stem: The epoch shown is recorded in a warm room from a patient under two blankets. What is the most likely cause of the abnormal activity?
questions.rationale: Slow, high-amplitude drifting waves across several EEG and EOG channels in a warm patient are typical of sweat artifact, which changes the skin-electrode potential. Cooling the room and removing blankets usually helps.
questions.reference: Standard PSG technology texts.

image.alt: N2 epoch with large, slow, rolling waves of about one cycle every 4 seconds in all EEG and EOG channels, much larger than the background.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Slow, rolling waves of about one cycle every 4 seconds across all EEG and EOG channels, far larger than the background.

evidence.takeaway: Very slow drift on many channels in a warm patient is sweat. Cool the patient and room.

questions.stem: The amplifier calibration signal shown is recorded before a study. The time from the start of the pulse to point B is used to verify the channel's
questions.rationale: When a square-wave pulse is applied, the trace decays back toward baseline. The time to fall to about 37% of the peak is the time constant, which is set by the low-frequency filter. A shorter time constant means a higher low-frequency filter setting.
questions.reference: PSG instrumentation texts on amplifier calibration.

image.alt: Amplifier calibration square wave. Point A marks the peak of the deflection; point B marks where the signal has decayed to about 37% of its peak.

questions.topic: Airflow sensors for apnea vs hypopnea
questions.stem: During a diagnostic PSG, which sensor is recommended to score apneas?
questions.rationale: The oronasal thermal sensor is the recommended sensor for apneas, and the nasal pressure transducer for hypopneas. RIP sum or nasal pressure is an alternative if the thermal signal fails.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, respiratory rules (sensors).

questions.sectionName: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.stem: Which patient is the best candidate for a home sleep apnea test?
options: A 70-year-old with heart failure and an ejection fraction of 25%
A 48-year-old with loud snoring, witnessed apneas, and sleepiness, without other major illness
questions.rationale: HSAT is meant for uncomplicated adults with a high pretest probability of moderate to severe OSA. Significant heart failure, opioid use (risk of central apnea), and children are reasons to choose in-lab PSG.
questions.reference: Kapur VK, et al. J Clin Sleep Med. 2017;13(3):479-504.

questions.sectionName: Perform procedures and follow practice guidelines
questions.stem: A split-night study is ordered. After 2 hours of recording, the AHI is 48 events per hour, and 4 hours remain before lights on. The technologist should
options: wait one more hour before deciding
continue the diagnostic study until morning
start CPAP titration per the split-night protocol
wake the patient and end the study
questions.rationale: An AHI of 40 or more after at least 2 hours of diagnostic recording meets split-night criteria, and more than 3 hours remain for titration. Starting titration now follows the protocol.
questions.reference: Kushida CA, et al. Sleep. 2005;28(4):499-521; AASM split-night guidance.

questions.stem: The epoch shown is from an adult. It should be scored as stage
questions.rationale: Alpha rhythm fills more than half the epoch over the occipital lead, with blinks and high chin tone. That meets the criteria for stage W.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, sleep staging rules.

image.alt: Epoch with 8 to 12 Hz rhythmic activity in O2-M1 throughout, eye blinks in the EOG channels, and high chin EMG.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Rhythmic 8 to 12 Hz alpha over the occipital lead through most of the epoch.
Eye blinks and high chin tone.

evidence.takeaway: Alpha in more than half the epoch, with blinks and high chin tone, is stage W.

questions.stem: The epoch shown is from an adult. It should be scored as stage
questions.rationale: Alpha is present for less than half the epoch and is replaced by low-amplitude 4 to 7 Hz activity, with slow eye movements and a vertex sharp wave. There are no spindles or K-complexes for N2.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, sleep staging rules.

image.alt: Epoch with alpha only in the first several seconds, then low-amplitude 4 to 7 Hz activity, slow rolling eye movements, and a vertex sharp wave.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Alpha only at the start of the epoch, less than half of it.
Then low-amplitude 4 to 7 Hz activity with slow rolling eye movements and a vertex sharp wave.

evidence.takeaway: Alpha replaced by low-amplitude mixed frequencies for most of the epoch, without spindles or K-complexes, is N1.

questions.stem: The 30-second tracing shown is from a 5-year-old during N2. Nasal pressure falls about 50% for about 4 breaths (10 seconds), followed by a 4% desaturation. How should it be scored?
options: No event, because it lasts only 10 seconds
questions.rationale: Pediatric hypopneas need a 30% or greater drop in flow for at least 2 breaths with a 3% desaturation or an arousal. Duration in seconds isn't the criterion in children; breath count is.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, pediatric respiratory rules.

image.alt: 30-second pediatric tracing at about 24 breaths per minute where nasal pressure falls by about half for four breaths, followed by an SpO2 drop of about 4% and an arousal.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Nasal pressure falls about 50% for about four breaths.

evidence.takeaway: In children, a 30% drop for 2 or more breaths with a 3% desaturation or arousal is a hypopnea.

questions.stem: The tracing shown is from a 6-year-old during N2. Airflow and effort both stop for 7 seconds (about 3 missed breaths), followed by a 4% desaturation. How should this be scored?
options: No event, because it lasts less than 20 seconds
questions.rationale: In children, a central apnea can be scored if it lasts at least 20 seconds, or if it lasts at least 2 missed breaths and is associated with an arousal or a 3% or greater desaturation. Here a 4% desaturation follows a 3-breath pause.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, pediatric respiratory rules.

image.alt: 30-second pediatric tracing with a 7-second pause in which airflow and both effort belts are flat, followed by an SpO2 drop of about 4%.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Airflow and effort both stop for about 7 seconds, about 3 missed breaths.

evidence.takeaway: A pediatric central pause of 2 or more breaths with a 3% desaturation (or arousal) is a central apnea.

questions.stem: Data from a PSG are shown.
questions.rationale: PLMS index = PLMS × 60 ÷ TST in minutes = 150 × 60 ÷ 375 = 24 per hour. The PLM arousal index would be 40 × 60 ÷ 375 = 6.4 per hour.
questions.reference: AASM Scoring Manual v3, parameters to be reported.

questions.stem: During a CPAP titration in an adult at 8 cm H2O, the 2-minute view shown is recorded during N2. What should the technologist do?
options: Switch to bilevel PAP right away
Increase CPAP by at least 1 cm H2O
questions.rationale: For patients 12 and older, CPAP is increased by at least 1 cm H2O (no sooner than every 5 minutes) when at least 2 obstructive apneas are observed. Three obstructive apneas with desaturation show the pressure is still too low.
questions.reference: Kushida CA, et al. J Clin Sleep Med. 2008;4(2):157-171.

image.alt: Two-minute titration tracing at CPAP 8 cm H2O with three obstructive apneas of 17 to 20 seconds each, with continued and growing effort, snoring after each, and SpO2 drops of 6 to 7%.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Three pauses in PAP flow of 17 to 20 seconds each.
Effort continues through each pause, so they're obstructive.

evidence.takeaway: Two or more obstructive apneas in an adult means CPAP should go up by at least 1 cm H2O.

questions.topic: Download - APAP pressure for fixed CPAP
questions.stem: The 30-day APAP report shown is for an adult with uncomplicated OSA. The provider wants to switch to fixed CPAP. Which pressure is suggested by the data?
options: About 11 cm H2O, near the 90th percentile pressure
8 cm H2O, halfway through the range
questions.rationale: With good use, a low residual AHI, and low leak, the 90th (or 95th) percentile pressure, about 11 cm H2O here, is commonly used to choose a fixed CPAP pressure.
questions.reference: Morgenthaler TI, et al. Sleep. 2008;31(1):141-147.

image.alt: 30-day APAP report at 5 to 15 cm H2O with use about 7 hours a night, residual AHI about 2, low leak, and a 90th percentile pressure of about 11 cm H2O on the summary and daily graph.

questions.topic: O2 during titration - when to add
questions.stem: During a CPAP titration, the 2-minute REM view shown is recorded after obstructive events have been controlled at 10 cm H2O. SpO2 has stayed at about 87% for 8 minutes. What should the technologist do?
options: Wake the patient to end REM sleep
Add supplemental O2 at 1 L/min per protocol
questions.rationale: When SpO2 stays at 88% or less for 5 minutes or more without obstructive events, the AASM recommends adding O2, starting at 1 L/min. Raising pressure without obstructive events doesn't fix hypoxemia from lung disease or hypoventilation.
questions.reference: Kushida CA, et al. J Clin Sleep Med. 2008;4(2):157-171.

image.alt: Two-minute stage R tracing on CPAP 10 cm H2O with regular breathing, no apneas, hypopneas, or snoring, and SpO2 steady between about 86% and 88%.

evidence.label: tracing

marks.note: Regular breathing with no apneas, hypopneas, or snoring on CPAP 10.
SpO2 stays at about 86% to 88% anyway.

evidence.takeaway: Persistent SpO2 of 88% or less for 5 minutes or more without obstructive events means add O2 at 1 L/min.

questions.stem: How does a mandibular advancement oral appliance treat OSA?
options: It keeps the patient from rolling onto the back during sleep
It holds the lower jaw forward, enlarging the airway behind the tongue
It stimulates the hypoglossal nerve to move the tongue forward
It delivers pressurized air through the mouth to splint the airway
questions.rationale: Mandibular advancement devices position the lower jaw and tongue forward, which enlarges the upper airway and reduces collapse during sleep.
questions.reference: Ramar K, et al. AASM/AADSM oral appliance guideline. J Clin Sleep Med. 2015;11(7):773-827.

questions.stem: What is the first-line treatment for most otherwise healthy children with OSA and enlarged tonsils?
questions.rationale: Adenotonsillectomy is first-line for children with OSA and adenotonsillar hypertrophy. CPAP is used if surgery isn't an option or OSA persists afterward.
questions.reference: Marcus CL, et al. Pediatrics. 2012;130(3):e714-e755.
